answers.q: Is GPU execution faster for any tested neuroevolution configuration?
answers.a: YES (confirmed): GPU sequential execution was faster than CPU sequential at large/P4/S50/hetero: 1.13x (95% CI 1.06-1.21, n=3 GPU / 3 CPU reps); large/P8/S50/hetero: 1.15x (95% CI 1.08-1.21, n=3 GPU / 3 CPU reps). Cross-strategy (best available strategy on each device, exploration data): GPU ahead at large/P4/S50/hetero (seq vs seq, 1.16x).

answers.q: At what workload sizes does GPU execution become competitive?
answers.a: GPU reached >= 50% of CPU throughput (a definition of 'competitive', not a measurement) at: large/P4/S50/hetero (1.13x), large/P8/S20/hetero (0.59x), large/P8/S50/hetero (1.15x). Confirmed crossover along model size (mean parameters) between 103281 and 2.45997e+06 (interpolated ~2.02e+06). Tier 'small': no break-even from the fitted model (GPU per-step cost is not lower than CPU's). Tier 'medium': no break-even from the fitted model (GPU per-step cost is not lower than CPU's). ESTIMATED (model extrapolation, not measured) break-even for tier 'large': ~43 training steps per individual (inside the tested range).

cpu/small: per-model fixed work (construct+trace+first execution+fitness) 89%, training 7%, GA+cleanup 4.0%, unattributed 0.0%; cpu/medium: per-model fixed work (construct+trace+first execution+fitness) 73%, training 25%, GA+cleanup 2.1%, unattributed 0.0%; cpu/large: per-model fixed work (construct+trace+first execution+fitness) 17%, training 83%, GA+cleanup 0.4%, unattributed 0.0%; gpu/small: per-model fixed work (construct+trace+first execution+fitness) 96%, training 4%, GA+cleanup 0.4%, unattributed 0.0%; gpu/medium: per-model fixed work (construct+trace+first execution+fitness) 92%, training 7%, GA+cleanup 0.4%, unattributed 0.0%; gpu/large: per-model fixed work (construct+trace+first execution+fitness) 90%, training 10%, GA+cleanup 0.4%, unattributed 0.0%

answers.q: Does GPU batching materially improve throughput?
answers.a: Batched vs sequential on the SAME device and workload (cross-strategy): homogeneous populations GPU 1.96-2.01x (n=2), CPU 1.97-1.98x (n=2); heterogeneous populations GPU 1.36-1.41x (n=2), CPU 1.33-1.39x (n=2); only 40% of heterogeneous individuals fell into a batchable bucket (median).

answers.q: How does memory usage scale with population and model complexity?
answers.a: Largest additional memory in any completed configuration: 3.46 GB (gpu-batched, large, P=32, homo); maximum swap growth 0 MB. sequential strategies discard each model so their peak depends on model size, not population.

answers.q: What evidence supports or contradicts the proposed crossover?
answers.a: 3 point(s) have confirmation repetitions. Crossover status: confirmed. Confirmation agreed with exploration within 25% wherever both exist. A crossover is claimed only where adjacent confirmed points changed from CPU-faster to GPU-faster.

answers.q: Which findings are specific to TensorFlow Metal and this M1 Pro?
answers.a: Observed on this software/hardware combination only: per-model graph tracing/first execution accounts for 91% of GPU wall time at its worst tier, consistent with a per-model compilation/dispatch cost on tensorflow-metal; strict-placement kernel gaps are reported in the block table; results are valid only for the recorded TensorFlow / tensorflow-metal versions and `--grappler` setting. Whether this cost is a Metal-plugin limitation or a property of the M1 Pro GPU is NOT separable with this experiment.

only 3 independent repetitions per confirmed point (wide intervals); one machine, one session; day-to-day variance (up to ~6% on throughput in earlier baselines) is not included in the CIs; cold vs warm Metal shader cache can change first-execution cost between sessions; break-even steps are model extrapolations; synthetic regression task and small dense networks only; paired comparisons use identical genomes/data but GPU reductions are not bit-reproducible; 0 configuration(s) did not complete and 11 were skipped by the budget/limits.
